content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on grass as the standard biblical image for the transience, frailty, and mortality of human life — humanity flourishes briefly then withers, in contrast to God's eternal word (Isa 40:6-8; Ps 90; Ps 103; 1 Pet 1:24; Jas 1:10-11). Secondary uses include divine provision (Matt 6:30; Ps 23:2), the short-lived wicked, and abundance/multitude; Response C notes as a minority reading that grass represents people/humanity itself ('the people is grass').","book_summary":"The book identifies grass as the individual mortal — a man, flesh — and situates that mortal within 'the field God farms unto harvest,' pairing Isaiah 40:6-8 (all flesh is grass) with Matthew 13:38 (the field is the world), thereby framing grass not merely as an emblem of brevity but as the individual person growing in God's world-field awaiting eschatological harvest.","consensus_core_identification":"Grass symbolizes the brevity, frailty, and mortality of human life/flesh in contrast to God's permanence.","book_core_identification":"Grass is the individual mortal human being (a man, flesh), conceived as a plant in the field (the world) that God cultivates toward harvest.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus treats grass chiefly as a simile for the quality of transience attaching to humanity in general; the book converts this into a direct identification — grass IS the individual mortal — and adds an agrarian-eschatological frame absent from all consensus responses: the mortal as a crop in the world-field God farms unto harvest (via Matt 13:38). This reclassifies grass passages from illustrations of brevity into references to individual persons within a divine harvest scheme, and narrows the referent from 'human life/glory' as an abstract quality to the concrete individual man.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book retains the consensus's central referent — grass corresponds to mortal human flesh, grounded in the same anchor text (Isa 40:6-8, 'all flesh is grass... surely the people is grass'). Response C even lists 'grass represents humanity or peoples' as a minority alternative. But the book materially changes precision and framing: it individualizes the referent ('a man'), shifts emphasis from the quality of transience to the identity of the person, and imports a harvest/field-cultivation dimension (Matt 13:38) that no consensus response associates with grass. This is boundary-level disagreement and reconfiguration, not replacement of the referent, so REFINED rather than DIVERGENT; it is too materially altered (especially the harvest-field element) to be MATCH.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: Isaiah 40:7 itself says 'the people is grass,' so grass=mortal man is simply the literal core of the consensus's own proof text, and 'the field God farms unto harvest' is an interpretive elaboration rather than a change in identification. Conversely, one could argue the Matt 13:38 harvest-field component is sufficiently absent from all consensus responses to push toward NOVEL for that half of the entry.","confidence":"medium"}
